"Dysbiosis" refers to an imbalance in the gut microbiota characterised by shifts in microbial populations and reduced species diversity. This imbalance is commonly observed at the onset of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
Dysbiosis can lead to alterations in the gut environment, including increased inflammation and impaired barrier function, which may contribute to the progression of IBD.

Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder triggered by the ingestion of gluten in genetically predisposed individuals. The immune response leads to damage in the small intestine, causing malabsorption, diarrhea, and poor appetite. On histopathological examination, crypt hyperplasia, villous atrophy, and increased CD8+ T lymphocytes in the lamina propria are classic features of celiac disease.
**Celiac disease:**
**Definition:** Autoimmune disorder triggered by ingesting gluten-containing foods in genetically susceptible individuals.
**Synonym:** Gluten-sensitive enteropathy, Celiac sprue
**Diagnosis:** Biopsy of the second part of the duodenum or proximal jejunum
**Serum markers:**

items.text: Anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG)-most sensitive
Anti-endomysial antibodies (EMA)-most specific

blocks.text: **Histology:**

items.text: Increased intraepithelial CD8+ T lymphocytes (intraepithelial lymphocytosis),
Crypt hyperplasia (increased mitosis)
Villous atrophy (reduced mucosal surface area, causing malabsorption)
Inflammatory cells infiltration

blocks.text: **Environmental enteropathy (Option A):** is a condition marked by chronic inflammation and structural changes in the small intestine. It is commonly seen in individuals from regions with poor sanitation and hygiene.

**Whipple's disease (Option C):** is a rare bacterial infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei. It primarily affects the small intestine but can also involve other organs. The biopsy findings in Whipple's disease are different and typically show PAS-positive macrophages.

**Chronic pancreatitis (Option D):** is characterised by persistent inflammation and fibrosis of the pancreas, leading to impaired pancreatic function. It can cause malabsorption, but the biopsy would not show the characteristic findings of celiac disease, such as villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia.
Uveitis

Ulcerative colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) with possible extraintestinal manifestations. HLA-B27–positive patients have a higher risk of certain autoimmune complications, particularly in the eye. The most classic ocular manifestation is acute anterior uveitis.
**Features of uveitis in HLA-B27–associated IBD:** Usually unilateral, sudden onset.
**Symptoms:** eye pain, redness, photophobia, blurred vision.
**Exam:** ciliary flush, cells & flare in anterior chamber. Can be recurrent.

**Conjunctivitis (Option B):** It is more common in reactive arthritis (Reiter’s syndrome), not as strong an association with ulcerative colitis. Conjunctivitis involves superficial eye redness without the deep inflammation of uveitis.
**Scleritis (Option C):** Deep, boring eye pain; associated with systemic autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis. It is less commonly seen in ulcerative colitis.
**Iridocyclitis (Option D):** refers to inflammation of the iris and ciliary body (a subset of anterior uveitis).
HNPCC / Lynch syndrome is caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes.
The most commonly affected genes are:

items.text: MLH1
MSH2
MSH6
PMS2

blocks.text: Loss of these MMR proteins → failure to correct base-pairing errors → microsatellite instability (MSI) → increased risk of colorectal cancer (esp. right-sided) and extra-colonic cancers (endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urinary tract).

Lynch syndrome is associated with germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, leading to microsatellite instability (MSI). MSI is a hallmark of Lynch syndrome-associated tumours, including colorectal adenocarcinoma.
**APC (Option A):** tumor suppressor gene mutated in Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP), not Lynch syndrome.
**MYC (Option C):** proto-oncogene involved in Burkitt lymphoma (t(8;14)), not colorectal cancer syndromes.
**TERT1 (Option D):** encodes telomerase reverse transcriptase; mutations linked to certain familial cancers but not HNPCC.
**Barrett's oesophagus is a complication of chronic GERD, characterised by intestinal metaplasia (Option B):** in the oesophageal squamous mucosa. It increases the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
Occurs in 10% of individuals with symptomatic GERD. Affects up to 2% of the general population. Most common in white males, typically between ages 40 and 60.

**Cancer Risk:** Increases the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma. The majority of oesophageal adenocarcinomas are associated with Barrett's oesophagus, but not all individuals with it will develop cancer.

Recognised as red, velvety mucosa (Barrett's mucosa) extending upward from the gastroesophageal junction & alternating with pale squamous mucosa and light-brown gastric mucosa. Subclassified as long segment (≥3 cm) or short segment (<3 cm). Short-segment disease carries a lower cancer risk compared to long-segment disease.

Intestinal-type metaplasia with goblet cells replacing squamous epithelium. Goblet cells are diagnostic of Barrett oesophagus and have distinct mucous vacuoles that stain blue with Alcian blue. This imparts the shape of a wine goblet to the remaining cytoplasm. Goblet cells are diagnostic, with pale blue mucous vacuoles resembling a wine goblet. Non-goblet columnar cells, like gastric-type foveolar cells, may also be present.
**Incorrect Options: Columnar to squamous (Option A):** occurs in squamous metaplasia (e.g., chronic irritation in bronchi of smokers), not Barrett’s.
**Transitional to squamous (Option C):** occurs in the bladder with chronic irritation (e.g., schistosomiasis).
**Cuboidal to columnar (Option D):** not typical in Barrett’s; cuboidal epithelium is seen in small ducts/glands, not in the oesophagus.

Ferroportin is an iron exporter protein found on the surface of cells, including enterocytes in the intestine. Hepcidin binds to ferroportin and induces its internalization and degradation. This leads to a decrease in iron export from the enterocyte into the plasma, thereby reducing iron absorption and availability.
**Incorrect Options:**

items.text: **Option A. Transferrin:** Transferrin is a protein that binds to iron in the plasma and facilitates its transport. Hepcidin does not directly bind to transferrin. Instead, hepcidin regulates iron levels by binding to ferroportin.

**Option C. Ferritin:** Ferritin is an intracellular protein that stores iron. Hepcidin does not directly bind to ferritin. Instead, hepcidin regulates iron levels by modulating the activity of ferroportin, which in turn affects iron release from ferritin.

**Option D. Divalent metal transporter 1:** Divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) is a transmembrane protein responsible for the uptake of iron from the lumen of the intestine into enterocytes. Hepcidin does not bind to DMT1. Its main target is ferroportin, which is involved in the release of iron from the enterocyte into the bloodstream.

blocks.text: The primary cellular change seen in Barrett's oesophagus is metaplasia of squamous epithelium into intestinal/columnar epithelium.
**Incorrect Options:**

items.text: **Squamous Metaplasia (Option A):** is the replacement of normal columnar epithelium with stratified squamous epithelium, typically due to chronic irritation (e.g., bronchial epithelium in smokers or the cervix). In Barrett's oesophagus, the reverse occurs, with squamous epithelium replaced by columnar epithelium.

**Severe Dysplasia (Option B):** is disordered cellular growth and a precancerous condition. In Barrett's oesophagus, dysplasia (low-grade or high-grade) may arise as a progression from intestinal metaplasia toward adenocarcinoma, but it is not a defining feature-rather, a complication.
**Cuboidal Metaplasia (Option D):** is not a recognised feature of Barrett's oesophagus or any other oesophagal condition.

blocks.text: Barrett's oesophagus is specifically defined by intestinal metaplasia, with goblet cells present within the columnar epithelium.
The clinical presentation and HPE image showing characteristic cystically dilated crypts & glands are suggestive of Juvenile polyp.
**Juvenile Polyps:**
**Occurrence:** Common in children under 5 years old; can be sporadic or syndromic.
**Size & Appearance:** Typically less than 3 cm, pedunculated, smooth-surfaced, reddish with cystic spaces.
**Histology:** Dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory debris, mixed inflammatory infiltrates, and sometimes attenuated muscularis mucosae.
**Pathogenesis:** Linked to mucosal hyperplasia; mutations in SMAD4 and BMPR1A (TGF-β pathway).
**Dysplasia:** Rare in sporadic polyps but present in juvenile polyposis syndrome.
**Complications:** Juvenile polyposis syndrome can lead to colonic adenocarcinoma (30-50% risk by age 45).

**Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (Option A):** is an autosomal dominant condition characterised by hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract. While rectal polyps may occur in this syndrome, the histopathological image seen in this case is more indicative of juvenile polyps.
**Villous Adenoma (Option B):** are adenomatous polyps commonly seen in adults, characterised by finger-like projections with abundant mucin production.
**Tubular Adenoma (Option D):** are common adenomatous polyps found in adults, characterized by glandular structures with tubular architecture.

**Myxoid liposarcoma:** The presence of a retroperitoneal mass with the molecular finding of t(12;16) translocation & image showing abundant ground substance, with branching capillaries and few immature adipocytes, is highly suggestive of Myxoid liposarcoma.
Liposarcoma, malignant tumours of adipose tissue, is the most common type of sarcoma in adults.
These tumours typically arise in the deep soft tissues of the proximal extremities and retroperitoneum, commonly affecting individuals in their sixth and seventh decades of life.
**Pathogenesis:** The three subtypes of liposarcoma—well-differentiated, myxoid, and pleomorphic—have distinct genetic abnormalities:

items.text: **Well-differentiated liposarcomas** exhibit amplifications in the chromosome region 12q13–q15, which includes the p53 inhibitor MDM2.
**Myxoid liposarcomas** are characterised by a fusion gene caused by a t(12;16) translocation, which arrests adipocyte differentiation, leading to uncontrolled proliferation of primitive cells.
**Pleomorphic liposarcomas** display complex karyotypes without consistent genetic abnormalities.

blocks.text: **Histopathological findings:**

items.text: Well-differentiated liposarcomas are composed primarily of mature adipocytes with scattered atypical spindle cells.
Myxoid liposarcomas are characterised by a rich basophilic extracellular matrix, arborizing capillaries, and primitive cells at different stages of adipocyte differentiation, resembling fetal fat.
Pleomorphic liposarcomas feature sheets of anaplastic cells with bizarre nuclei intermixed with varying numbers of immature adipocytes, called lipoblasts.

blocks.text: **Lipomas (Option B):** are benign tumours made up of mature adipose tissue. They are typically well-defined and do not show the cellular atypia or genetic abnormalities associated with liposarcomas.
**Spindle Lipoma (Option C):** is a benign variant of lipoma characterised by spindle-shaped cells within the fatty tissue. It lacks the genetic mutations seen in myxoid liposarcoma.

**Polymorphic Lipoma (Option D):** , also referred to as pleomorphic lipoma, is a benign lipomatous tumour made of mature adipose tissue containing various cell types. It does not exhibit the specific t(12;16) translocation found in myxoid liposarcoma.

The clinical presentation & the bird beak sign on barium swallow suggests achalasia, a condition characterized by the inability of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax and an absence of peristalsis in the distal esophagus. It is caused by a decreased release of nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), which are essential for smooth muscle relaxation. This results in increased tone of the LES and impaired peristalsis.
**Achalasia:**
**Pathology:** Incomplete LES relaxation/Increased LES tone/Aperistalsis of the esophagus
**Symptoms:** Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), Difficulty in belching, Chest pain

**Primary Achalasia:** It is caused by degeneration of nitric oxide-producing neurons that normally induce LES relaxation. Degeneration of the extraesophageal vagus nerve or dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus may occur.
**Secondary Achalasia:** Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi infection) destroys the myenteric plexus, leading to peristalsis failure and esophageal dilation.
**Associated with conditions like:**

items.text: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy
Infiltrative disorders (e.g., malignancy, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis )
Systemic sclerosis
Dorsal motor nuclei lesions (post-polio)
Down syndrome or Allgrove syndrome (achalasia, alacrima, ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency).

blocks.text: Some cases linked to HSV1 infection, immunoregulatory gene polymorphisms, Sjögren syndrome, or autoimmune thyroid disease, suggesting immune-mediated destruction of inhibitory esophageal neurons.
**Treatment:**

items.text: Laparoscopic myotomy
Pneumatic balloon dilation
Botulinum neurotoxin (Botox) injections to inhibit cholinergic neuron contraction.

blocks.text: Hirschsprung disease arises when the migration of neural crest cells is arrested, causing a lack of ganglion cells (Option B ruled out) in the affected segment, leading to a lack of peristalsis in the affected bowel segment, causing functional obstruction and bowel dilation without inflammation or strictures (Option D ruled out). This leads to aganglionosis, preventing peristalsis and causing bowel dilation.

**Morphology:** Histopathological confirmation involves identifying the absence of ganglion cells, and acetylcholinesterase staining aids in diagnosis. The disease typically involves the rectum, with short-segment or long-segment Hirschsprung disease based on the extent of involvement.
**Clinical Features:** Symptoms include failure to pass meconium, abdominal distension, constipation, and bilious vomiting.
Complications such as enterocolitis, perforation, and peritonitis can occur. Surgical resection of the aganglionic segment is the primary treatment.

**Acquired Megacolon:** Acquired Megacolon, seen in conditions like Chagas disease and ulcerative colitis, may share a similar pathophysiology with Hirschsprung disease, particularly in cases involving the loss of ganglion cells.
**Visceral myopathy (Option C):** refers to smooth muscle dysfunction, which can affect gastrointestinal motility but is not the cause of Hirschsprung disease.

blocks.text: **Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome:**
**Inheritance:** Autosomal dominant.
**Age of Onset:** Median age of 11 years.
**Key Features:**

items.text: Multiple GI hamartomatous polyps.
Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation (dark macules on lips, buccal mucosa, palms, genitalia, and perianal region).
Polyps are most common in the small intestine but may also occur in the stomach, colon, bladder, and lungs.

blocks.text: **Complications:** Risk of intussusception, potentially fatal.
Increased cancer risk (lifetime risk ~40%), including cancers of the GI tract, testes, pancreas, breast, lung, ovarian, and uterus.
**Pathogenesis:** It is caused by germline mutations in the STK11 gene, a tumour suppressor gene regulating cell polarization and growth. Somatic loss of the second STK11 gene copy in cancers.
**Morphology:** Polyps are pedunculated and lobulated.
Histology shows an arborizing network of smooth muscle, connective tissue, lamina propria, and glands.

Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigmental epithelium is not typically associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHTPE) is more commonly seen in other conditions, such as familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).

The isthmus of the gastric pits contains stem cells, which are responsible for replenishing the various cell types in the gastric mucosa. These stem cells differentiate into different types of gastric cells, including parietal cells, chief cells, and mucous cells, as they migrate along the pit.
